slides.headline: How to use *Wispr Flow* to type with your voice

slides.heading: 1. *2,000 words* a week free
paras: The free plan covers 2,000 words a week on Mac and Windows. After that it slows down until Sunday.
Pro is $15 a month or $144 a year for unlimited dictation.

slides.heading: 2. Hold *Fn* and talk
paras: Click where you want the text, hold Fn on a Mac (Ctrl and Win on Windows), speak, then let go.
Double-tap the shortcut to dictate hands-free.

slides.heading: 3. Teach it *your words*
paras: Add names and jargon in the Dictionary so Flow spells them right.
If it keeps getting one word wrong, add a correction that swaps the wrong spelling for yours.

slides.heading: 4. Edit by voice with *Command Mode*
paras: Turn it on in Settings, Experimental. Select text, hold Fn and Ctrl, and say what to change.
Flow rewrites the text in place. It needs Pro or a trial.

site_article.headline: How to use Wispr Flow on Mac and Windows: voice typing with AI, step by step
site_article.dek: Wispr Flow turns speech into clean text in any app. Here is how to set it up, the shortcuts that matter, what the free plan covers and where it falls short.
site_article.summary: Wispr Flow is an AI dictation app that types what you say into any text field on Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android, removing filler words and adding punctuation. The free plan gives 2,000 words a week on desktop; Pro costs $15 a month or $144 a year.
site_article.seo_title: How to use Wispr Flow on Mac and Windows (free plan explained)
site_article.seo_description: How to use Wispr Flow: setup, the Fn and Ctrl+Win shortcuts, hands-free mode, Dictionary, Command Mode, and what the free 2,000 words a week get you.
site_article.answer_summary: Install Wispr Flow, sign in, allow the microphone (and Accessibility on Mac), then click into any text box, hold Fn on a Mac or your chosen shortcut on Windows, speak and release. The text appears where your cursor is.
site_article.hero_alt: Promotional image of the Wispr Flow dictation app on an Android phone.

paragraphs.text: How to use Wispr Flow, in short: put your cursor where you want text, hold one shortcut key, talk, and let go. Flow turns what you said into cleaned up text and drops it into whatever app you are in, according to Wispr's help center. It removes filler words, adds punctuation and handles it when you correct yourself mid-sentence. It runs on Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android, and it needs an internet connection because transcription happens in the cloud.

It is not a niche tool anymore. Wispr AI raised $280 million in August 2026 at a $2 billion valuation, and the company says users have written more than 60 billion words with Flow, according to SiliconANGLE. This guide covers setup, the shortcuts worth learning, the free plan and the honest downsides.
Wispr Flow free plan and prices

The free plan gives you 2,000 words a week on Mac and Windows, with a hard cap of 5,000. Past 2,000, Flow slows down; at the cap, dictation stops until the weekly reset at midnight Pacific time on Sunday. iPhone and Android share a separate weekly allowance, according to Wispr's plans page.

Pro costs $15 a month or $144 a year, which works out to about $12 a month, and removes the word limit. A default trial lasts 14 days, and students with a recognized .edu address can get longer trials. Team plans start at $23 per user per month. Prices outside the US are set in local currency, so they may differ.
Two thousand words is roughly a handful of long emails. Use the free week to test whether you actually dictate every day before you pay for unlimited.
How to set up Wispr Flow on Mac and Windows

paragraphs.title: 1. Download and open Flow
paragraphs.text: Get the app from wisprflow.ai/download. On a Mac, move it to Applications and open it; a menu bar icon shows it is running. On Windows, run the installer and open Flow from the Start menu; it lives in the system tray.

paragraphs.title: 2. Sign in
paragraphs.text: Click Sign in via browser and use Google, Apple, Microsoft, SSO or email. If your company uses SSO, check with IT first instead of making a separate account.

paragraphs.title: 3. Allow the microphone
paragraphs.text: Flow asks for microphone access on both systems, plus Accessibility on a Mac so it can type into other apps. If you clicked deny, turn it on under System Settings, Privacy and Security on a Mac, or Settings, Privacy and Security, Microphone on Windows. Use Test your microphone to check that it hears you.

paragraphs.title: 4. Pick your shortcut and languages
paragraphs.text: On a Mac with an fn key, the default is fn. On a Mac without one, it is Ctrl and Option. On Windows the help center lists Ctrl and Win as the default, and you can change it with Edit shortcut. Pick your languages or leave automatic detection on; Flow supports more than 100 languages and you can mix them in one sentence.

paragraphs.title: 5. Do your first dictation
paragraphs.text: Click into any text box, an email, a chat, a doc. Press and hold your shortcut, speak normally, then release. On desktop the text appears after you let go, not word by word as you talk.

paragraphs.title: 6. Go hands-free for long text
paragraphs.text: Double-tap your shortcut to start hands-free dictation, so you do not have to hold the key for a long message.
Make Wispr Flow spell your words right

The Dictionary is where you teach Flow names, product terms and jargon. On Mac or Windows, open Dictionary in the left sidebar, click Add new, type the word and click Add word. Then dictate a sentence with it to check. If Flow keeps writing the same wrong spelling, add a correction: turn on Correct a misspelling and enter the wrong version Flow produces.

On desktop Flow can also learn words by itself when the auto-learn setting is on and you fix dictated text. It skips everyday words, numbers, web addresses and very famous names. You can import up to 1,000 entries from a file on Mac and Windows.
Edit text by voice with Command Mode

Command Mode lets you speak an instruction instead of text: edit what you wrote, draft a reply or run a web search. It is off by default; turn it on under Settings, Experimental. The default shortcut is Fn and Ctrl on a Mac and Ctrl, Win and Alt on Windows. The help center ties it to Pro, active trials and enterprise plans.

paragraphs.title: Command 1: Tighten a message
paragraphs.text: Make this shorter and friendlier, and keep the dates.

paragraphs.title: Command 2: Fix the tone
paragraphs.text: Rewrite this so it sounds professional, not annoyed.

paragraphs.title: Command 3: Draft a reply
paragraphs.text: Write a short reply that says yes to Thursday and asks for the agenda.

Hold the Command Mode shortcut, say the instruction with no wake word, and release. Press Esc to cancel. Asking it to build a website or an app only gives you drafted text, not a working app, the help center notes.
What Wispr Flow is bad at

There is no offline mode: everything goes through the cloud, so a bad connection means no dictation. A May 2026 review by Spokenly, which makes a rival app, also says the AI cleanup sometimes over-edits what you said, real-world delay is about one to two seconds, and data sharing for model training is on unless you opt out. Wispr's onboarding asks for your data preference, so read that screen instead of clicking through.

Flow is worth it if you write a lot of email, chat and notes and talk faster than you type. If you mostly write code, numbers or work offline, the free week will show you quickly that it is not your tool.
